prompt.context: A recent Columbia MBA graduate, Finn Russo, is exploring entrepreneurial opportunities and has decided he would like to open up a private boating marina near Sullivan's Island, South Carolina. With limited knowledge of the region apart from celebrating a bachelor party in the Charleston area and some online research, Finn has chosen a potential location and has come to you for guidance on how to proceed. He has one financial partner (his father) who is contributing $2,000,000 to the project interest free to be paid back in the 3rd year of operation.
prompt.question: Should Finn open up a marina?

clarifying_info.q: What is a slip vs. a mooring?
clarifying_info.a: Docking (wet slips) is docking space near shore, usually with electrical power supplied, charged based on $/foot of boat length. Mooring is a permanent anchor spot in the water some distance from shore, mostly used for larger boats and sailboats.

clarifying_info.q: What are the primary and alternative sources of revenue?
clarifying_info.a: Primary revenue comes from docking and mooring. Alternative sources include selling boating supplies and equipment, boat repairs, and selling fuel.

clarifying_info.q: Does the marina offer both daily and monthly options?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, the marina will be offering both monthly and daily moorings and slips.

clarifying_info.q: Does Finn have experience in boating or running a marina?
clarifying_info.a: No, Finn has no experience in boating or running a marina.

exhibits.title: Marina Pricing Chart
exhibits.shows: A table showing the number of slips and moorings and their daily and monthly prices

exhibits.title: Occupancy and Use
exhibits.shows: A table showing the daily and monthly occupancy rates for slips and moorings, average boat size, and annual occupancy assumption

exhibits.title: Marina Costs
exhibits.shows: A breakdown of initial setup costs and ongoing annual costs for the marina

framework: 1. Profitability: Revenue (# of slips, # of moorings, demand/occupancy, price) and Costs (development, wages, maintenance, real estate)
2. Market: Market size, type of customer/boats, seasonality (warm vs. cold months)
3. Other considerations: Regulatory environment, insurance, security, weather risks, option to purchase existing marina

questions.prompt: What is the potential revenue in Year 1? (Use Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2)
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask about demand after seeing the pricing exhibit, prompting Exhibit 2. Candidate should notice the larger discount for monthly users. Assume a year has 300 days for daily calculations and 10 months for monthly calculations.

math.setup: Calculate slip and mooring revenue separately for daily and monthly, then sum. Slips: price per foot x boat length x occupancy x count x time. Moorings: flat price x occupancy x count x time.
steps: Slip daily revenue: 40 slips x 50% daily use x 40 ft x $2/ft x 300 days = $480,000
Slip monthly revenue: 40 slips x 40 ft x $40/ft x 50% x 10 months = $320,000
Mooring daily revenue: 50 moorings x 25% daily use x $60 x 300 days = $225,000
Mooring monthly revenue: 50 moorings x 75% monthly use x $1,000 x 10 months = $375,000

questions.prompt: What will SeaBag Marina's profitability be over 3 years? (Use Exhibit 3)
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask for costs and clarify revenue/cost growth assumptions. Assume revenue grows 10% annually but costs remain flat. The $2,000,000 loan from Finn's father is part of the $3,000,000 setup cost, not an additional charge. The remaining $1,000,000 of setup cost is Finn's own equity. The loan must be repaid in Year 3.

math.setup: Project revenue for Years 1-3 with 10% annual growth. Sum total costs: $2M loan (repaid Y3) + $1M equity setup + $500K/year ongoing costs x 3 years. Compare 3-year cumulative revenue to 3-year cumulative costs.

brainstorming.prompt: What risks or next steps should Finn consider before proceeding?

categories.name: Weather & Location Risks
ideas: Hurricane exposure near Sullivan's Island, South Carolina
Need to evaluate whether the chosen location is safe from severe weather events
Finn has done minimal research on the specific location chosen

categories.name: Operational Risks
ideas: Finn has no marina or boating experience — is he suited to run the establishment himself?
Can the marina bring in fuel, which is a common and expected marina offering?
Insurance requirements for a marina operation

categories.name: Competitive & Demand Risks
ideas: Limited competitive analysis around the area — demand assumptions may not hold
Seasonality could affect occupancy beyond the 300-day/10-month assumptions

categories.name: Regulatory Risks
ideas: Permitting and environmental regulations for waterfront/marina development

recommendation: Yes, Finn should open the marina. He will be profitable within 3 years, generating $134,000 in cumulative profit after repaying the $2M loan and covering all setup and operating costs.
The marina generates significantly more revenue than ongoing costs; the longer it operates, the higher the cumulative profit.
risks: Weather and hurricane risk given the coastal South Carolina location
Finn's lack of marina experience raises execution risk
Revenue projections assume stable occupancy — competitive dynamics or seasonality could undermine demand
next_steps: Dig further into the exact location Finn has chosen, given his minimal prior research
Conduct a competitive analysis of marinas in the Sullivan's Island/Charleston area to validate demand assumptions
Look into insurance requirements and relevant coastal/environmental regulations before proceeding
